“Not Every Shiny Robot Is a Solution.”
Photo of Andrew Rosenblum
By Andrew Rosenblum
Apr 27, 2026

Graphic by Adam Dixon
As agtech venture dollars dry up, a new study suggests tech companies focus on tools that are affordable and easy for farmers to use.
Back in 2023, California-based startup FarmWise released a product that promised to upend modern agriculture: a next-generation, AI-enabled weeding robot called Vulcan, able to distinguish weeds from crops and then kill the interlopers, using computer-controlled blades. FarmWise’s MIT- and Stanford-trained founders had more than “a solution in search of a problem” — by virtually all accounts, this was an effective solution to the weeds that cost American farmers billions each year. Particularly given the rise of “superweeds” that had evolved immunity to common herbicide formulations —not to mention more than 100,000 lawsuits alleging that Bayer’s Roundup caused cancer. Both Time magazine and the World Ag Expo named FarmWise weeders to their “best of” lists.

And yet, FarmWise’s Vulcan proved too capital-intensive for most farmers and wound down operations last year — in spite of raising $65 million in venture funding. The company sold its assets to an investor, the produce giant Taylor Farms.
FarmWise is one of nearly 20 agtech startups around the world forced to cease operations in 2025, according to a new University of Nebraska-Lincoln white paper. Authors Ankit Chandra and Ishani Lal blamed a “cost adoption mismatch” between expensive and complex agricultural tech and what farmers can reasonably afford and incorporate into daily operations. Chandra estimates that given low prices and high input costs, producers of row crops like corn or soy can afford to invest only about $4 per acre before new tech starts to become too pricey.
That said, the news is not all bad for high-tech on the farm. The authors found continued resilience in agtech startups whose products required low capital expenditure by farmers and were easy to use.
A Tough Row to Hoe
Four dollars an acre might sound like a low limit, given that a competent farmer can produce 200 bushels of corn on that land, which would fetch over $800 at today’s prices. But Chandra said that the costs of farm inputs and labor all can add up to make farmers feel strapped at the prospect of incorporating another high-tech gadget.
“The farmer doesn’t have that amount to invest into new technologies, even if there [is] beneficial impact around saving inputs or conserving the ecosystem,” he said. “So there is a cost adoption mismatch.”
Andy Jobman is a Nebraska corn and soybean farmer who spoke with Offrange while taking a break from strip tilling his fields. He thinks less of a particular dollar limit on new tech than in terms of return on investment. But the savings have to be obvious.
> “The farmer doesn’t have that amount to invest into new technologies, even if there [is] beneficial impact around saving inputs or conserving the ecosystem.“
“If I’m investing $4 an acre, if I’m getting back $20, then it’s a no-brainer to invest in it, right? [But] where is that generating my increased profitability? Is it through higher yields? Can I actually yield the same with less inputs, or actually do more with less inputs?”
Chandra said the $4 figure for 2025 comes in part from talking to farmers themselves — and that the situation may be even worse this year. “Just in the last couple of weeks, a few of them [said], ‘We are forecasting our next year yields, the net returns look negative to us. So how do we invest into new technologies?”
Jobman said that during difficult times, farmers tend to tighten their spending and reduce any excess spending to a bare minimum. “When things are really tough, that really doesn’t make you want to open your pocketbook to try too many new things,” he said. “That’s not a bad thing either. It really makes you take an even harder look at what you’re doing and say, ‘Okay, is what I’m doing really sustainable?’”
Hard Times
Chandra and Lal published their paper in January, analyzing 18 agtech shutdowns that occurred in 2025. Ag and food tech venture investment worldwide peaked in 2021 at almost $11 billion, before falling to $6 billion last year, largely fueled by concerns about paths to profitability and the long period for agtech investments to pay off in the face of higher interest rates. The most hard-hit category was indoor vertical farms — six of these companies failed around the world. Vertical farms require a lot of energy and generally yield products that have to compete with inexpensive, conventionally produced crops like lettuce. Three different makers of insect protein — as a low-carbon-footprint source of livestock feed, pet food, or fertilizer — also failed. And in addition to the FarmWise weeder in the ag robotics category, the drone chemical spray company Guardian Agriculture also went under.
After the paper was published, autonomous tractor company Monarch Tractor burned through more than $240 million in venture investment, laid off all employees, and announced its shutdown was imminent. Monarch’s self-driving tractor was also on Time’s top inventions list, while Forbes magazine predicted the company would be a billion-dollar startup. But between a price tag of upwards of $100,000 and persistent reports of inconsistent performance, the company couldn’t make the math work.
Meanwhile, in a recent blog post, an Iowa popcorn producer railed against the way that AI and robotics companies can take away decision-making from farmers and fieldworkers — while seeking to hoover up data using opaque terms of service agreements. “Not every robot is a shiny solution,” the post concluded.
> “The average row crop farm is at least 1,000 acres in size. So that’s just not necessarily scalable, you know, unless you had an army of those machines.“
Chandra said it’s not that advanced robotics tech doesn’t work, but that there is a mismatch between the high upfront hardware costs of bleeding-edge tech and the tight margins under which farmers operate.
Eight months ago, as part of its acquisition publicity, Taylor Farms announced that it had deployed FarmWise autonomous weeders in rows of lettuce, vegetables, and melons in Salinas, and managed to weed 100 acres in a week, using two of the machines.
For the corn and soy farmer Andy Jobman, each autonomous weeder doing 50 acres/week is too slow for the vast row crop fields of the Midwest. “That’s not even close to the scalability that Midwest row croppers need,” Jobman said. “The average row crop farm is at least 1,000 acres in size. So that’s just not necessarily scalable, you know, unless you had an army of those machines out there, right? Yeah, at that point, it’s probably cost-prohibitive.”
Green Shoots for Affordable Agtech
Chandra and Lal did find agtech companies to be optimistic about. They saw success for inexpensive AI analytics and sensing; financial software targeted toward the ways that farm operations already borrow and spend; and certain biological additives. In general, these agtech winners don’t require heavy capital expenditure, or “capex,” in contrast with leasing or buying a robot or vertical farming infrastructure. They also have less of what the authors call “adoption friction,” meaning that they don’t require learning complex new tech skills or dramatically changing the way a farmer works. (Disclosure: The owner of Offrange is Ambrook, which offers ag-focused accounting software. Ambrook was not mentioned in the report).
Sarah Evanega, a former Cornell ag scientist who has gone to work for a tech-oriented apple producer30082-1/fulltext?ref=ambrook) called Okanagan Specialty Fruits in Washington state, has had success with a relatively low capex sensor that offers AI analysis and guidance. A “smart” camera attached to a farm vehicle has been a game-changer for the spring process of culling unpromising fruit, Evanega said.
“Their cameras aren’t just snapping pictures; they’re running full-blown AI, right there mounted on our ATV or tractor, while our guys drive through the orchard,” Evanega said. “They’re processing every tree on 500 football fields’ worth of trees, and we get instant detailed information about our apples — from bud to harvest. It feels more sci-fi than farming.”
In a process called “thinning,” farmers use a chemical agent to kill off less promising fruit in the spring and early summer, causing the tree to direct its energy to the most promising apples for the harvest. (Growers will also thin trees by hand too, though that is even more time-consuming). The tool, called the XV3 and made by a company called Vivid Machines, provides a map about the current state of an apple crop — including recommendations on which of the nascent apples called “fruitlets” should be culled. This resulted in a 40-50% savings on the chemical spray used for the thinning, while producing fruit and yield of the same quality as conventional thinning, according to a Penn State study.
> “You’re not paying overtime because you’re sending people only to the places that they need to go.”
Vivid Machines charged $5,000+ per acre for this data last year, according to Lancaster Farming News. CEO Jenny Lemieux echoed the point from Andy Jobman that farmers care less about the cost if the savings on materials or labor are demonstrably higher, whether for the thinning process, for predicting yields, or other actionable data provided by the device. “Maybe it saves you on the amount of nitrogen you’re going to spread, or it helps you be more efficient with your crews,” she said. “Maybe you’re not paying overtime because you’re sending people only to the places that they need to go.”
Chandra said that specialty crops are a better bet for high-tech capital investment because higher prices give farmers more leeway to experiment.
But Jon Clements, an extension tree fruit specialist at UMass Amherst, who favorably reviewed the XV3 in analyzing his crop load in 2024, said that apple growers have become more price-sensitive too.
“It is not all roses with apples these days either as over-production and increased costs have made margins very thin,” Clements said, in an email. “Five or six years ago there was more willingness to invest in this kind of tech but that has waned somewhat here at the moment.”
In the meantime, not all of the investment into the shuttered agtech startups was money wasted. FarmWise may be no more, but Vulcan weeders continue to roll through the fields of Salinas. The problem for FarmWise was financial, not technical. There’s still interest in an autonomous machines that eliminates the need for herbicide or tedious fieldwork – just not at an MSRP of $645,000.

Top Fundraising Tools Every Startup Should Try

Top Fundraising Tools Every Startup Should Try
Table of Contents
Arrow Down
Fundraising is hard enough without twenty tabs open, five spreadsheets out of sync, and investor notes scattered across random docs. The right fundraising tools will not magically close your round, but they can save you from chaos, slow follow ups, and missed opportunities.
Today, investors expect startups to run their fundraising like a real process, not a one-off scramble. That means tracking every touchpoint, sending clean updates, managing your data room properly, and staying on top of your cap table and pipeline. Trying to do all of that manually is how things slip through the cracks.
This article walks through the top fundraising tools every startup should try, from investor CRMs and outreach platforms to data room, modeling, and cap table tools. You will see what each tool is actually useful for, when to introduce it, and how to avoid bloating your stack with shiny software you do not need.
Why Startup Fundraising Platforms Matter
The fundraising ecosystem is undergoing a seismic shift, with startups facing heightened competition and evolving investor expectations. Here are the top fundraising platforms for startups: Base Templates, Qubit Capital, Foundersuite, WeFunder, SeedBlink, Funden, and OpenVC. Each helps founders secure capital quickly and efficiently.
1. Prepare your pitch deck
2. Choose your fundraising platform
3. Build investor list
4. Outreach using platform tools
5. Track investor communications
6. Review feedback and iterate
If a platform doesn’t fit your needs, try local angel networks or hybrid funding approaches, and prepare alternative outreach methods.
Using Warm Introduction Intelligence
Building on smarter investor matching, warm introduction intelligence tools help founders identify mutual connections for targeted outreach. These platforms analyze existing networks to suggest the most effective introduction paths. By prioritizing warm introductions, startups can improve investor response rates and reduce the time spent on cold outreach. This approach streamlines the fundraising process and enhances engagement quality.
Venture capital funding has changed. There are fewer deals, but check sizes are larger. This creates a challenging environment for early-stage companies. Despite volatility, startups on Carta combined to raise $89 billion in new funding in 2024. This marked an 18.4% increase from the previous year. Access to advanced fundraising tools clearly correlates with capital raised, reflecting why platforms are essential for growth.
The impact of choosing the right fundraising platform is evident from real market results. Startups leveraging Carta as a fundraising tool collectively secured $89 billion in new funding in 2024, an 18.4% year-over-year increase. This outcome underscores that advanced platforms directly support capital-raising at significant scale.

7 Startup Fundraising Platforms & Tools to Accelerate Growth
Securing funding is a critical milestone for startups, and the right tools can make all the difference in streamlining the process. From pitch deck creation to investor outreach management, these seven startup fundraising platforms are designed to support startups at every stage of their journey. Whether you're preparing for your first funding round or scaling toward Series A, these tools offer tailored solutions to accelerate growth. Startups that leverage these platforms report a 25% faster fundraising cycle and a 15% increase in investor engagement, according to a recent survey by Startup Genome.
Making tool selection critical, 3 out of 4 startups fail within the first year. Many collapse from poor market adaptation or resource gaps. Strategic platform use can help founders sidestep these pitfalls as they pursue growth.
1. Base Templates: Simplify Pitch Deck Creation
Creating a compelling pitch deck is often the first step in fundraising, and Base Templates makes this process effortless. This platform provides professionally designed pitch deck templates, term sheet templates, and an investor search tool, all accessible via an intuitive dashboard. Ideal for early-stage startups that have raised less than $1MM, Base Templates ensures your fundraising documents are polished and persuasive. In 2024, over 5,000 startups used Base Templates to secure pre-seed and seed funding, with notable success stories including the SaaS company Notion, which credits its early fundraising momentum to a well-structured deck built on this platform.
2. Qubit Capital: Holistic Fundraising Guidance
Startups benefit from hands-on fundraising support with Qubit, from investor outreach to refining strategic growth plans. Backed by a vast network and personalized guidance, founders gain the insights needed to secure funding efficiently. Qubit Capital’s approach includes tailored investor introductions, pitch review sessions, and ongoing mentorship, resulting in a 30% higher funding success rate for clients compared to industry averages.
3. Foundersuite: Manage Investor Outreach
For startups preparing for Series A, Foundersuite provides a feature-rich CRM platform tailored to fundraising. With extensive capabilities for tracking investor outreach and managing communication, this tool is perfect for startups aiming to raise $5MM or more. Foundersuite introduced AI-powered follow-up reminders and analytics dashboards, helping companies like fintech startup Brex manage over 200 investor relationships simultaneously and close their $300 million Series C round efficiently.
4. WeFunder: Build Investor Communities
Consumer-facing startups can benefit greatly from WeFunder, a platform designed to foster community-driven funding rounds. By enabling shared funding management, WeFunder simplifies coordination among investors and helps startups build lasting relationships. In 2024, beverage brand Recess raised $3 million from over 2,000 individual investors on WeFunder, demonstrating the power of community engagement in scaling consumer brands.
5. SeedBlink: Target European Investors
European startups with limited VC connections will find SeedBlink invaluable. This equity management and investment platform offers comprehensive features for matching with investors, though it comes with higher fees and equity costs. SeedBlink facilitated over €150 million in investments for European tech startups, including the Romanian AI company Druid, which closed a €30 million Series B round through the platform’s investor syndication tools. Investor syndication tools' are platform features that allow multiple investors to invest together or share deal opportunities.
6. Funden: Personalized Investor Introductions
Startups in the early stages of fundraising can benefit from Funden’s focus on social introductions and assisted fundraising. Even if your startup lacks measurable success metrics, Funden’s personalized connections can help you secure the right investors. In 2024, healthtech startup MindLabs used Funden to connect with angel investors, resulting in a successful $2 million pre-seed round despite limited initial traction.
7. Open VC: Accelerate Pitch Deck Sharing
Open VC simplifies the process of sharing pitch decks with investors, offering advanced AI-powered deck review and matching features. This tool is particularly useful for founders looking to optimize their outreach and receive actionable feedback. Open VC reported that startups using its AI review feature reduced time-to-meeting by 20%, with companies like logistics startup Sennder leveraging the platform to secure introductions to top-tier European VCs.
Centralizing Fundraising Workflows for Efficiency
 Create a single repository for all fundraising documents to ensure easy access and version control for your team.
 Use pipeline tracking tools to monitor investor interactions and follow-up tasks in real time.
 Grant stakeholders appropriate access to documents and updates, enhancing transparency and alignment throughout the fundraising process.
Top VC & Angel Investor Networks for Startups
Finding the right startup fundraising platform is pivotal for startups seeking early-stage capital. These startup fundraising platforms, such as AngelList and Crunchbase, streamline investor connections.
1. AngelList: Simplifying Angel Investing with Roll-Up Vehicles
AngelList has revolutionized how startups connect with angel investors. Through its innovative roll-up vehicles, this platform aggregates multiple angel investors into a single entity, simplifying the investment process for founders. Startups can integrate AngelList listings to connect with targeted angel investors, making it easier to secure funding while minimizing administrative complexities. In 2024, SaaS startup Levels raised $12 million from over 100 angels using AngelList’s roll-up vehicle, reducing legal costs and streamlining cap table management.
'Roll-up vehicle' means a legal structure that combines multiple investors into one entity for startup investment.
2. Crunchbase: A Comprehensive Investor Research Tool
Crunchbase stands out as a robust database for researching investors and tracking funding histories. Its searchable interface allows startups to identify investors based on industry focus, investment size, and previous funding rounds. Crunchbase data feeds can be used to analyze investor trends for smarter outreach strategies. The platform’s integration with LinkedIn and Salesforce enables seamless workflow management, and companies like fintech startup Ramp have credited Crunchbase’s analytics for helping them identify and close with strategic investors during their $300 million Series D round.
3. Angel Capital Association: Connecting Startups with Angel Groups
The Angel Capital Association (ACA) serves as a bridge between startups and over 250 angel groups across the U.S. By fostering connections with these networks, ACA enables targeted outreach to investors who align with specific industries or funding needs. This nonprofit fundraising platform also provides educational resources to help founders navigate the complexities of early-stage investing. In 2024, ACA-supported startups collectively raised over $1.2 billion, with notable exits including biotech firm Ginkgo Bioworks, which attributes its early funding success to ACA’s network.
Transparent Valuation Tools for Investor Negotiations
Building on the value of investor networks, transparent valuation tools empower startups to present clear, data-backed business worth. These platforms offer standardized methodologies and market benchmarks, reducing ambiguity during negotiations. By providing investors with transparent metrics, founders can foster trust and streamline due diligence. This approach ultimately increases the likelihood of successful funding agreements.
For startups facing challenges in securing funding, addressing fundraising challenges and solutions can help founders overcome obstacles with proven strategies, especially during periods of economic uncertainty.
Leading Equity Crowdfunding Platforms for Startups
Equity crowdfunding platforms are reshaping how startups raise capital, offering community-driven investment opportunities that appeal to both founders and investors. With the rise of consumer-facing startups, platforms like Republic, SeedInvest, and Wefunder are gaining traction as essential startup fundraising platforms.
Equity crowdfunding accounted for over $1.5 billion in startup funding in the U.S., according to Crowdfund Capital Advisors, with a growing number of B2B and SaaS companies also leveraging these platforms for growth capital.
1. Republic: Democratizing Startup Investments
Republic stands out for its inclusivity, allowing non-accredited investors to participate in funding rounds. Startups can raise between $50,000 and $5 million, tapping into a broad pool of contributors. This platform is particularly appealing for founders seeking community-backed funding without restrictive barriers. To maximize visibility, startups can embed Republic campaign links on their websites, encouraging wider participation. In 2024, fintech startup Mainvest raised $2.2 million from over 1,500 investors on Republic, using the platform’s marketing tools to drive campaign momentum and build a loyal customer base.
2. SeedInvest: A Quality-Driven Approach
SeedInvest prioritizes quality over quantity, employing a rigorous vetting process to ensure only high-potential startups make it onto the platform. This approach builds trust among investors, who can feel confident in the caliber of opportunities available. Founders benefit from access to a curated network of investors, making SeedInvest an excellent choice for startups aiming to stand out in a competitive market. SeedInvest reported a 70% increase in successful campaigns, with healthtech startup VirtuSense raising $5 million after passing the platform’s due diligence process.
3. Wefunder: The Largest Community-Driven Platform
Wefunder has earned its reputation as the largest equity crowdfunding platform in the U.S., enabling startups to host shared funding rounds. Its community-driven model fosters collaboration between founders and investors, creating a sense of shared purpose. This platform is ideal for startups looking to build strong relationships with their backers while raising substantial capital. In 2024, robotics startup FarmWise raised $4.5 million from over 3,000 investors on Wefunder, leveraging the platform’s storytelling and video features to engage a broad audience.
Equity crowdfunding is more than a trend, it’s a transformative tool for startups seeking alternative fundraising methods. Staying ahead of startup funding trends enables founders to identify emerging opportunities and adapt their fundraising strategies to evolving investor preferences.
Crowdfunding widgets and campaign links can be integrated into your website to engage a broader investor base, making these platforms even more impactful for startups. Companies like Allbirds and BrewDog have successfully used embedded crowdfunding campaigns to convert customers into investors, fueling both brand loyalty and capital growth.
Innovative Revenue-Based Financing Options for Growth
Revenue-based financing is reshaping how startups secure capital for growth, offering non-dilutive alternatives to traditional venture capital. Platforms like Clearco and Pipe have emerged as game-changers, enabling businesses to convert recurring revenue into upfront capital without sacrificing equity. Revenue-based financing deals grew by 28% year-over-year, according to CB Insights, as more SaaS and eCommerce startups seek flexible funding options that align with their cash flow cycles.
1. Clearco: Tailored Funding for SaaS and eCommerce
Clearco specializes in providing non-dilutive capital to SaaS and eCommerce startups. By repaying a percentage of revenue, businesses can access funding without giving up ownership. This model is particularly beneficial for companies with predictable revenue streams, allowing them to scale operations or invest in marketing. Clearco’s solutions integrate seamlessly into financial planning, offering startups a reliable way to convert monthly recurring revenue into growth opportunities. In 2024, DTC brand Haus used Clearco to access $1 million in growth capital, which was repaid through a share of sales, enabling rapid expansion without equity dilution.
2. Pipe: Unlocking Recurring Revenue
Pipe offers a unique solution for startups with recurring revenue models. It transforms monthly recurring revenue into upfront capital, enabling businesses to optimize cash flow without diluting equity. This approach is ideal for companies looking to accelerate growth while maintaining control. By integrating Pipe’s revenue financing APIs, startups can streamline their financial strategies and focus on scaling. SaaS company Capchase used Pipe to convert $2 million in annual contracts into immediate working capital, supporting product development and customer acquisition initiatives.
Flexible Alternatives to Venture Capital
Revenue-based financing is gaining traction as a flexible alternative to traditional VC funding. Profitable startups are increasingly adopting this model to scale sustainably while retaining ownership. The rise of platforms like Clearco and Pipe highlights evolving approaches to business financing.
A deeper look into startup fundraising strategies provides insights into securing capital in a changing market. Industry experts recommend combining revenue-based financing with traditional equity rounds to optimize capital structure and minimize dilution, as demonstrated by eCommerce brand Italic, which blended both approaches to fuel its international expansion.
Key Market Challenges in Startup Fundraising
Compounding the challenge, 49.4% of startups fail within their first five years, per 2024 U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data. These odds highlight why adapting to current funding realities is essential for founder survival. According to the National Venture Capital Association, the average time to close a seed round has increased to 5.2 months, underscoring the need for efficient processes and robust investor pipelines. Leveraging the right startup fundraising platform can help founders navigate these market challenges and secure funding more efficiently.
Declining VC and Pre-Seed Funding
The reduction in VC funding rounds underscores the need for startups to recalibrate their expectations. With fewer opportunities available, founders must prepare robust fundraising strategies to stand out. The sharp 36% decrease in pre-seed funding further emphasizes the challenges for early-stage startups. Incorporating this data into investor pitch decks can help founders address market realities and demonstrate resilience. For example, AI startup Runway included market contraction data in its 2024 Series A pitch, positioning itself as a resilient outlier and successfully raising $50 million despite the downturn.
The Investor Meeting Marathon
Securing funding often requires persistence. Early-stage founders typically need to meet with over 50 investors before closing a deal, according to a 2025 survey by DocSend. This daunting statistic highlights the necessity of planning an extensive outreach strategy. By preparing for multiple investor meetings, startups can increase their chances of finding the right fit for their vision and goals. Companies like Calendly have attributed their successful Series B round to a disciplined approach, tracking every investor interaction and iterating their pitch based on feedback from over 60 meetings.
Adapting to the Challenges
Startup fundraising platforms offer valuable tools to streamline the process, but startups must also focus on crafting compelling narratives and demonstrating market potential. As online donation platforms and alternative funding sources gain traction, founders might explore hybrid approaches that combine equity, debt, and revenue-based financing. Industry best practices suggest leveraging data-driven storytelling, transparent financials, and clear go-to-market strategies to stand out in investor meetings.
Understanding these challenges is the first step toward overcoming them. By addressing the realities of reduced funding opportunities and the need for extensive networking, startups can refine their approach and improve their chances of success. Building a resilient fundraising strategy is essential for navigating the evolving capital landscape.
For further guidance, fundraising best practices provide actionable steps for building investor confidence and maintaining momentum post-funding.
Conclusion
Adapting to evolving market trends, embracing AI-driven innovations, and utilizing diverse startup fundraising platforms are essential strategies for startups aiming to secure funding in a competitive environment. A well-rounded, data-driven approach not only enhances decision-making but also ensures that actionable insights are effectively integrated into your fundraising efforts. Project description
DE EN ES FR IT PL
Decision support system for sustainable agriculture and research
Climate change has already impacted several sectors, including agriculture and people’s lives, causing severe damage worldwide. Consequently, there is a crucial need for a better decision support system and management solutions for agriculture. The EU-funded FARMWISE project aims to transform the EU’s agriculture sector by providing farmers and decision-makers with a revolutionary decision support system using AI, remote sensing, and precision agriculture. Furthermore, the project will collaborate with European organisations to increase knowledge sharing and co-creation, develop novel AI-based tools for improved water monitoring and management, and assist farmers and researchers. Finally, to achieve this, FARMWISE will collaborate with researchers and stakeholders in the sector.
Objective
FARMWISE transforms the EU agricultural sector by empowering farmers and decision-makers with a state-of-the-art decision support system, combining precision agriculture, Artificial Intelligence, and remote sensing. FARMWISE provides new insights into water quality, quantity, soil health, and nutrient management.  
FARMWISE's state-of-the-art framework fosters knowledge sharing between scientists, farmers, and policymakers in a co-creation environment (Systems Thinking). It consolidates existing collaborations, and promotes new long-term cooperations between European organisations, including Water4All (BRGM) and Water Europe (SITES).  
The FARMWISE project will develop improved tools based on artificial intelligence (AI) for more efficient European water policy and decision-making founded on research-based technologies to solve the most burning water pollution and climate change problems. For this purpose, the FARMWISE consortium brings together the best European water, agricultural, climate, and AI researchers to handle the sustainability of water resources, the natural environment, and efficient agriculture in the highly diverse European landscape in view of present and future climate change. FARMWISE's impact will increase interest and bond cooperation of quadruple helix stakeholders for science-based solutions.  
FARMWISE evaluates, monitors, and implements gender and diversity balance in the consortium during the planned activities (T7.4). All partners' have established policies to foster gender equality, diversity, and inclusion for all employees. UEA holds a Silver Athena SWAN award in recognition of good practice in recruiting, retaining, and promoting women in STEMM subjects.

FARMWISE Indiana to continue local food mission as nonprofit
Friday, April 03, 2026
After nearly two years housed at Indiana University’s Environmental Resilience Institute (ERI), FARMWISE Indiana is taking the next step to ensure that locally produced food is accessible to more Hoosiers.
The program, launched in July 2024 to strengthen regional food systems in Indiana, is forming its own nonprofit organization, FARMWISE Indiana Inc. The new nonprofit officially started April 1 and will continue to serve farmers, food producers and buyers at schools, universities, and hospitals across the state.
“In less than two years, FARMWISE Indiana has proven there is strong interest at Indiana institutions to source more food locally,” said ERI Managing Director Sarah Mincey. “The technical assistance provided by FARMWISE Indiana’s team of value chain professionals is the key to unlocking that potential, helping to align farmers’ production with institutions’ food needs.
“ERI is proud to have served as an incubator for FARMWISE Indiana and will continue to serve as a bridge for food-system scholars and IU students as the program spins off into a standalone nonprofit. We look forward to continued collaboration.”

Members of the FARMWISE Indiana team. Beginning April 2026, FARMWISE Indiana started its own nonprofit to advance its local food mission.
Since its inception, the FARMWISE Indiana team has fostered relationships with more than 2,200 stakeholders, attended and hosted more than 1,200 meetings, and made more than 300 introductions between buyers and sellers of local food.
FARMWISE Indiana has spurred 247 businesses to work on their values-based procurement plans and has helped shift $75,000 to local farms.
In addition, FARMWISE Indiana is now able to quantify the direct farm impact of the institutions purchasing locally grown foods. For example, IU Dining in Bloomington spent more than $4 million buying food from Hoosier businesses, including $1.4 million from Indiana farms, during the 2024-25 academic year.
As a nonprofit with funding from Builders’ Vision, FARMWISE Indiana Inc. will continue to build on its early momentum and offer consulting services for farmers and food producers who are ready to sell wholesale but need guidance.
“FARMWISE Indiana Inc. will be successful because of the support received at Indiana University Bloomington and the university’s all-in approach to serving our state,” said FARMWISE Indiana Resilient Food Systems Manager Jodee Smith, who will be leading the new nonprofit. “IU has made major strides in providing service to improve the lives and livelihoods of Hoosiers. We are proud to launch this nonprofit from a place where colleagues are passionate about progress and support for all Hoosiers.”
About the Environmental Resilience Institute
The Environmental Resilience Institute, a CIMS (Centrally Administered Centers, Institutes, Museums and Service Centers) under IU Research, bridges academia, applied research, and community resilience to deliver the science-informed, equity-centered solutions needed to flourish in a changing climate. Through community partnerships, transformative research, and immersive learning, ERI is creating a more sustainable and prosperous future. Learn more at eri.iu.edu.

A few word about our methodology
As you can see, we built a database that ranks startups in the AgriTech market based on their total cumulative fundraising. To create this ranking, we reviewed many sources and cross-checked information across multiple places.
Whenever possible, we prioritized official company communications, since they are the most reliable source for funding amounts. When those were not available, we relied on reputable industry sources such as TechCrunch, Crunchbase, Financial Times or Forbes (to name a few).
We excluded random blogs, unverified websites, and any sources that could not be validated.
When AgriTech funding rounds were announced in other currencies such as euros, Swiss francs, Singapore dollars, Australian dollars, or rupees, we converted them into approximate USD equivalents for consistency.
Sometimes different sources report slightly different numbers, or the exact round size is not fully disclosed. In those cases, we flag the uncertainty and assign a confidence label to each startup, visible in the last column.
Here is what they mean.
Full confidence: The company’s equity fundraising history can be reconstructed completely from public sources. The rounds, dates, amounts, and key investors are clearly identified, with no meaningful gaps.
Strong confidence: The fundraising history is largely complete and reliable. There may be a small missing detail, such as incomplete investor information or a minor round with limited data, but the overall record is clear.
Partial confidence: The main fundraising rounds can be identified, but the record is incomplete or somewhat mixed. Some rounds may be missing or certain funding events may be difficult to separate clearly.
Low confidence: Public information is too limited, inconsistent, or ambiguous to reliably reconstruct the company’s equity fundraising history.
When the confidence level is too low, we take a conservative approach and exclude the company from the ranking. We don’t want to include data that cannot be reliably verified.
This reflects how we conduct all our research, including the work behind our report covering the AgriTech market.
In a world where LLMs hallucinate and unreliable information is everywhere, our goal is simple: provide data you can trust.
If you want the full detail on a specific calculation, feel free to contact us and we will gladly explain.
Finally, know that we update the dataset once per month, so come back here if you need fresh information.

On the other side, LLMs and random blog posts give you confident answers with no sources, and sometimes they just make things up. So we decided to fix the experience. For each market we cover, we build a structured database and update it on a regular basis. We track funding rounds, fund memos, M&A moves, partnerships, new products, policy changes, and the real activity of startups and incumbents. Then we turn all of that into a clear “market pitch” that shows where the opportunities are and how people actually win in that space.
Every key data point is checked, sourced, and put back into context by our team. That’s how we can give you both speed and reliability: fast coverage of new markets, without the usual guesswork.
